title: NYC Water: An Engineering Marvel
summary: Josh and Chuck explore New York City's tap water: its history from New Amsterdam ponds and tea water pumps, the cholera epidemics and the Croton Reservoir, the Great Fire of 1835, the Catskill and Delaware watersheds and aqueducts (including Tunnel No. 3), the EPA filtration waiver, how water is protected and treated (alum, filters, UV), water quality issues like turbidity, phosphorus runoff and disinfection byproducts, and whether NYC water explains the city's bagels and pizza. The episode closes with a listener mail story about house rolling in Franklin, Tennessee, and a sign-off with live show plugs.

segments.title: Live show plug and episode intro
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck promote an upcoming Seattle live show at the Paramount Theater, then introduce the episode on New York City's tap water.

segments.title: NYC tap water reputation and scale
segments.summary: The hosts describe New Yorkers' pride in their tap water and the city's water system delivering more than a billion gallons daily. They note that about ten percent of the water is filtered and the rest is unfiltered, one of only five major US cities with an EPA waiver, alongside Seattle, Portland, San Francisco and Boston.
topics: largest water system in the United States

segments.title: Early New York water: ponds, pumps and cholera
segments.summary: Early New Amsterdam relied on ponds and springs, including the Collect Pond, which was polluted by tanneries and waste. Public pumps and tea water pumps served the city, and the 1832 cholera epidemic pushed the city to look outside for cleaner water, leading to the Croton Reservoir.

segments.title: Canal Street origins and Aaron Burr's water company
segments.summary: A failed canal built to drain the polluted Collect became Canal Street after it was covered. Aaron Burr's Manhattan Company built an early reservoir with wooden log pipes, and the water was poor; the hosts describe it as a scam that helped found what became Chase Manhattan Bank.

segments.title: Great Fire of 1835 and the Croton system
segments.summary: The Great Fire of 1835 destroyed about seventeen city blocks in Lower Manhattan, with two deaths, partly because cisterns had been drained by earlier smaller fires. This spurred the faster completion of the Croton Reservoir, which opened mid-century with about ninety million gallons a day, plus the Murray Hill Reservoir.

segments.title: Growth and the Catskill and Delaware watersheds
segments.summary: As the city grew, including the five boroughs and over three million people by the turn of the century, it looked upstate to the Catskill and Delaware watersheds. The hosts explain what a watershed is and describe how these two systems form the source of New York's water.

segments.title: Catskill Aqueduct and Delaware Aqueduct
segments.summary: The 92-mile Catskill Aqueduct carries water to the city, crossing under the Hudson River about eleven feet below sea level using gravity and pressure, since the bedrock was deeper than expected. The 85-mile Delaware Aqueduct is described as the longest continuous tunnel in the world, built with steam shovels and dynamite. Tunnel No. 3 is still under construction and will allow the other tunnels to be drained for inspection.

segments.title: Watershed protection, land purchases and filtration cost
segments.summary: The hosts explain why New York protects its watersheds rather than filtering: a filtration plant would cost roughly ten billion dollars plus a hundred million a year to operate. The city owns large land holdings upstate, upgrades wastewater facilities, reimburses septic tank replacement, and plants saplings. The Croton watershed, which is now partly filtered, is the lesson learned.

segments.title: Treatment steps, sampling and water quality concerns
segments.summary: Water is chlorinated and UV-treated, with thousands of samples taken yearly and robotic buoys on the Kensico Reservoir. Hundreds of gray sampling stations are scattered around the city. The filtered ten percent uses alum, sand and anthracite filters, and UV. Concerns include turbidity, phosphorus runoff causing algae, and disinfection byproducts such as chloroform, which is above the national average but below legal limits.

segments.title: Bagels, pizza and water hardness
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether New York's naturally soft water makes its bagels and pizza better. The American Chemical Society calls the water the Goldilocks of bagel water, but the hosts conclude that technique and yeast handling matter more, with water contributing a small amount.

segments.title: Listener mail: house rolling in Franklin, Tennessee
segments.summary: Listener Brandon Saunders shares a story about rolling the house of country singer Brad Paisley when they were teens in Franklin, Tennessee, and how Paisley was friendly when his tour bus arrived.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to get in touch through the website or email and sign off.
